transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2026-08-05 15:00 PT
- Duration: ~62 minutes
- Attendees: Samir Patel / Erin Cho (Redwood), Liam Reed (Redwood CSM), Maya Singh / Carlos Ortiz / Priya Desai (Vertex)

Summary (auto):
Redwood SE explained KV-cache eviction algorithm, how prefix reuse affects effective hit rate, and what causes paging under long-context workloads. We discussed memory budgeting, kernel selection, quantization tradeoffs, and on-prem constraints (NVRAM / disk paging). Action items and POC plan captured at the end.

----- Transcript -----
[00:00] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out the time. we wanted to dig into the KV cache issues you've been seeing in staging — eviction, paging, prefix reuse — Erin's going to lead the deep dive.
[00:22] Maya: thanks Samir. yes, we've been seeing cache evictions mid-session when we hit long contexts, and then tail latency spikes while the model pages back in. it's pretty disruptive for our multi-turn assistants.
[00:35] Erin: totally get it. quick sanity check: are you running the on-prem package or Dedicated in cloud? and what's your sequence length profile, like median vs 95th?
[00:48] Carlos: on-prem appliance, VPC limited, we have NVMe local but limited RAM per GPU node. seq length median is ~512 tokens, 95th around 4096 for a subset of sessions, and we do continuous streaming so KV grows quickly.
[01:10] Erin: okay that explains a lot. when you have a heavy tail at 4k and continuous streaming the KV cache required per session balloons — most runtimes keep per-layer KV for autoregressive decoding. the eviction policy is usually LRU-ish by prefix + session id, and if you have many concurrent sessions with few large contexts you get eviction churn.
[01:40] Priya: can you explain churn a bit more? like why eviction would cause paging?
[01:50] Erin: sure. two pathways: first, eviction frees GPU memory but the runtime may page cold KV to host RAM or NVMe as a fallback to avoid recomputing KV. that paging is expensive and async so you see latency spikes when it reads back. second, frequent evictions mean that subsequent requests need to recompute KV from scratch which costs compute and increases token latency. so either way performance suffers.
[02:20] Maya: we suspected that. we also saw cases where prefix reuse didn't seem to hit even though sessions shared a lot of initial context. is that a keying issue?
[02:32] Erin: could be. prefix reuse depends on how you form cache keys. if your key includes session id or per-request nonce you won't get reuse. ideal is to key on normalized prefix tokens or a hash of the canonicalized prompt prefix. also watch out for whitespace/tokenization mismatches — different tokenizers or inconsistent normalization will fragment the cache.
[03:00] Carlos: we do add a small per-request metadata header right now, maybe that's poisoning the key.
[03:06] Erin: yep that would. quick suggestion: keep session-scoped metadata out of the cache key; store it in a separate routing layer. use a deterministic canonicalizer for the prefix (lowercase? remove timestamps?) then hash.
[03:20] Samir: besides keying, what other knobs do teams usually tweak?
[03:26] Erin: size of the per-GPU cache, eviction thresholds (percentages), fall-back policy (do you page to host vs recompute), and grouping small sessions into a shared prefix pool. also batching and kernel selection matter — higher batching improves throughput but increases peak memory for KV. quantization reduces memory per KV entry but sometimes at cost of quality or kernel compatibility.
[03:55] Priya: about paging: can Redwood avoid paging to NVMe at all if we tune correctly?
[04:02] Erin: yes you can avoid paging by either increasing GPU memory headroom (bigger GPUs or reduce batch/seq) or by increasing local host RAM used as a hot cache; we have an option to disable NVMe spill and instead prioritize recompute, which trades compute cycles for predictable latency. depends on which resource you want to spend.
[04:28] Maya: what's the recommended starting config for our profile (median 512, tail 4k, concurrency ~80 sessions)?
[04:36] Erin: preliminary rule-of-thumb: size per-session KV ~ layers * hidden_state * seq_len * bytes_per_param. with quantized KV you can reduce by ~2-4x. recommended starting: 1) enable prefix canonicalization and shared prefix buckets; 2) set eviction threshold at 75% GPU memory, trigger recompute for evicted sessions rather than NVMe paging; 3) cap per-session KV at 4k tokens but prefer prefix summarization for old context; 4) if you can, test 8-bit quantized KV (Q4) to reduce footprint. we'll send a config snippet.
[05:20] Carlos: that capping — won't truncating context change output? we can't just throw away early tokens.
[05:28] Erin: right — two approaches: hard truncate which loses earlier context, or summarize/condense prefixes into a smaller latent representation to keep semantics. Redwood supports prefix condensing as an experimental mode — it creates a condensed key that approximates earlier context, trades a bit of fidelity for memory savings. for critical flows, you should identify truly necessary prefixes and keep those in a persistent prefix store.
[05:55] Priya: curious — how does quantization interact with prefix reuse? any gotchas?
[06:02] Erin: quantization changes the bit representation of KV and can alter kernel choices. as long as you consistently quantize the values and use compatible kernels, reuse is fine; the gotcha is mixed-kernel environments. if part of your fleet runs Q4 kernels and another runs full precision, cache entries may not be interchangeable. ensure homogeneous runtime or versioned cache keys that include quantization metadata.
[06:30] Samir: that matches other customers. what about batching? we batch aggressively at our edge which seems to increase memory pressure.
[06:39] Erin: batching increases peak KV memory because you materialize more KV at once. two mitigations: dynamic batching (cap batch by memory footprint rather than number of requests) and continuous prefix reuse where you prioritize dispatching requests that share prefixes together to increase hit rate. Redwood's scheduler can be tuned to favor prefix-locality.
[07:05] Maya: interesting — is there a way to measure effective prefix reuse across sessions? we'd like to quantify the opportunity before we reorganize our prompts.
[07:14] Erin: yes, we provide a hit-rate heatmap in the console. but you can also dump hashed-prefix histograms from the runtime; the simplest is to log normalized prefix hash -> count per time-window, that gives you reuse frequency. Carlos, if you can supply a sample prefix corpus we can run that analysis.
[07:35] Carlos: will do. we'll extract top 50k prefixes and histograms.
[07:40] Priya: the paging spikes we saw — they correlate with certain time windows. could this be GC or other system-level noise?
[07:48] Erin: possibly. you should correlate eviction timestamps in runtime logs with system-level metrics: GPU mem pressure, host disk IO, kernel swap events. sometimes background jobs or backups can push NVMe IO contention which worsens read latency. also check per-process oom_kill logs.
[08:12] Maya: for on-prem, any KMS/HSM requirements that affect KV? we're using a hardware KMS for keys, but KV shouldn't be encrypted in GPU mem, right?
[08:22] Erin: correct, KV entries live in plaintext in GPU memory for performance. encryption-at-rest applies to spill files on disk; if you spill to NVMe you can mount encrypted volumes or use an encrypted spill path. the KMS integrates for keys/certs and we support HSM-based rotation flows. we'll attach the security whitepaper.
[08:47] Samir: let's talk about a reproducible experiment. if we run a POC, what's the minimal dataset and run steps?
[08:55] Erin: minimal POC: 1) supply a 24-hour trace with per-request tokenized prefixes + sequence lengths + session ids, 2) pick representative model (we recommend an open LLM that matches your production model), 3) run three configs: A) default cache + NVMe spill, B) tuned eviction + recompute (no NVMe spill), C) quantized KV + prefix condense. measure tail latency (p95, p99), token throughput, and effective hit rate. we'll provide the benchmark harness and dashboards.
[09:30] Carlos: for the trace, should we anonymize session ids?
[09:34] Erin: yes, anonymize but keep stable ids so prefix locality remains. tokenization must be preserved.
[09:42] Priya: what's the time to set up the dedicated test cluster? can we do within two weeks?
[09:47] Samir: we can spin a dedicated test cluster in 3–5 business days pending SOC docs and infra approvals. the long pole will be data prep.
[09:55] Maya: ok. we will prioritize the prefix corpus and trace.
[10:02] Erin: two more technical notes: 1) consider using a sharded prefix index for very large prefix sets — it reduces lookup contention, and 2) keep cache keys deterministic across rolling upgrades; include runtime version in key namespace to avoid incompatible reuse.
[10:20] Carlos: how do rolling kernels affect an active cache? we've seen mismatch after a driver update.
[10:27] Erin: driver/kernel mismatches can cause silent performance regression — best practice: drain or version namespace keys during upgrades. Redwood supports a versioned cache namespace param to force new keys after an upgrade window.
[10:42] Priya: about metrics to watch in prod — what are the top 6?
[10:48] Erin: hit rate, eviction rate (per-minute), page-in latency, recompute CPU/GPU time per token, memory pressure (GPU and host), and prefix uniqueness ratio. correlate with tail latency.
[11:05] Maya: can we get a sample dashboard?
[11:08] Erin: yes we'll provide the dashboard template and metric queries.
[11:12] Samir: quick note — some words in our runbook say "KV eviction is fine" but our product folks disagree. how do we reconcile?
[11:20] Erin: eviction is normal; the question is whether it triggers paging or recompute that you can't absorb. with the right policy you can make eviction a graceful reclaim rather than a noisy event. tune thresholds and prefer recompute for predictable latency, or increase hot-layer memory to avoid eviction for critical flows.
[11:40] Carlos: last deep question — prefix reuse across tenants: we have multi-tenant workloads; is it safe to share prefix pool?
[11:48] Erin: you can share but you must namespace keys per-tenant to avoid leaking cross-tenant semantics. shared pools for common system prompts are ok if you don't include sensitive tenant tokens. otherwise keep per-tenant buckets with a shared common prefix bucket for public prompts.
[12:05] Maya: thanks — that's helpful. any quick wins we can start with?
[12:10] Erin: quick wins: canonicalize prefix keys, disable NVMe spill for latency-sensitive flows and prefer recompute, enable prefix condensing on low-value flows, and test Q4 quantization on a staging subset. we'll send a prioritized checklist.
[12:26] Samir: great. let's recap next steps and owners.
[12:30] Maya: yep please share the config snippet and the benchmark harness link.
[12:34] Erin: will do. I'll attach kernel/config snippets plus the harness and the dashboard template.
[12:40] Samir: thanks everyone. we'll follow up once we have the trace and sample prefixes.
